1.title: Firewalls, Wireless, Embedded Systems and IoT
1.text: Welcome to Module ten: Firewalls, Wireless, Embedded Systems and I O T. It covers the exam area four. Networking and Cloud Security Concepts. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. four point one Understand network security: Firewalls (for example ports, applications). Wireless (for example Wi-Fi, Bluetooth). Embedded systems (for example Industrial Control System (I C S)), Internet of Things (I O T). Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: four. Networking and Cloud Security Concepts (twenty-one point three percent). Exam format: an adaptive exam of one hundred to one hundred twenty-five questions in two hours; a score of seven hundred on a scale of one to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official I S C two C C exam outline.

1.title: Firewalls
1.text: Firewalls. A firewall allows or blocks traffic by rules. Good rule sets use default deny: block everything, then allow only what is needed. Rules are read from the top, and the first match wins.

1.title: Firewalls, continued
1.text: Firewalls. The figure shows this: Firewall types from simple filters to application-aware devices.

1.title: Firewalls, continued
1.text: Firewalls. Packet filter (stateless). How it decides: Source and destination address, port, protocol of each packet. Note: Fast, simple; no memory of connections. Stateful inspection. How it decides: Tracks the state of each connection. Note: Allows replies to allowed requests. Proxy (application firewall). How it decides: Acts between client and server and understands the application. Note: Can filter content.

1.title: Firewalls, continued
1.text: Firewalls. Next-generation firewall (N G F W). How it decides: Adds application awareness, user identity, intrusion prevention, T L S inspection. Note: Decides by application, not only by port. Web application firewall (waff). How it decides: Protects web applications. Note: Blocks sequel injection and cross-site scripting. Host-based firewall. How it decides: Runs on one computer. Note: Protects that host. Exam tip: Stateless looks at each packet alone; stateful remembers the connection. A waff protects the web application; a network firewall protects the network edge.

1.title: Ports, applications and rule design
1.text: Ports, applications and rule design. Ports. Allow only needed ports (for example four forty-three for a web server). Applications. Modern firewalls identify the application even on an unusual port. Direction. Inbound rules protect servers; outbound (egress) rules stop data leaving and malware calling home. Implicit deny. The last rule denies everything not allowed. Intrusion detection system (I D S) detects and alerts; intrusion prevention system (I P S) detects and blocks. Network versions watch traffic; host versions watch one system. A I-assisted firewalls and I D S spot unusual behavior, not only known signatures.

1.title: Wireless: Wi-Fi
1.text: Wireless: Wi-Fi. W E P. Broken; never use. W P A. Old (T K I P); avoid. W P A two. A E S-C C M P; good if the passphrase is strong. W P A three. Newest; stronger key exchange (S A E), protects against offline guessing. Personal. One shared passphrase (pre-shared key). Enterprise. Each user logs in through eight oh two dot one X and a R A D I U S server; better for companies. Wi-Fi attacks: rogue access point (an unauthorized device on the network), evil twin (a fake copy of a real network), deauthentication floods, eavesdropping on open networks. Hiding the network name (S S I D) is not real security. Exam tip: Use W P A three or W P A two with a strong key, and enterprise login for companies. A rogue A P is an unauthorized device; an evil twin pretends to be a trusted one.

1.title: Bluetooth
1.text: Bluetooth. Bluetooth is a short-range wireless technology for headsets, keyboards and phones. Bluejacking. Sending unwanted messages to a nearby device. Bluesnarfing. Stealing data from a device without permission. Defenses: turn Bluetooth off when unused, do not accept unknown pairing requests, keep devices updated, avoid discoverable mode.

1.title: Embedded systems, ICS and IoT
1.text: Embedded systems, I C S and I O T. Embedded system. A computer built into a device for one purpose (printer, camera, car). Industrial control system (I C S). Systems that run industrial processes (factories, power); skay duh is one kind. Internet of Things (I O T). Networked everyday devices (sensors, cameras, smart locks). Default or weak credentials. Change defaults at install. Hard to patch, long life. Update firmware, retire unsupported devices. Little built-in security. Segment them on their own network; limit access. Unknown inventory. Keep an asset list; monitor traffic. In I C S, availability and safety come first, so patching is slow and careful. I O T botnets use weak devices to launch D dos (distributed denial of service) attacks. Exam tip: Isolate I O T and I C S from the corporate network and change default passwords. That is the answer to most I O T questions.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Which firewall remembers the state of each connection and allows replies to allowed requests? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: A stateful inspection firewall. A stateful firewall tracks connections; a stateless filter treats each packet alone.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A company wants to block sequel injection attempts against its public website. Which control fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: A web application firewall in front of the site. A web application firewall inspects web requests and blocks attacks such as sequel injection.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. An employee plugs an unauthorized wireless router into an office network port. What is this device called? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: A rogue access point on the network. An unauthorized access point connected to the network is a rogue access point.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. An attacker sets up a Wi-Fi network named like the airport network so travelers connect to it. What is this attack? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: An evil twin that imitates a trusted network. A fake network that copies the name of a real one is an evil twin.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A factory network contains old sensors that cannot be patched. What is the best protective step? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Place them on a separate segmented network. Unpatchable devices should be isolated by network segmentation.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Which Wi-Fi security protocol is the newest and gives the best protection of the choices? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: W P A three with a stronger key exchange. W P A three is the newest standard and protects better against offline guessing.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What does default deny mean? Answer: Block everything, then allow only what is needed. Question two. What does an I P S do that an I D S does not? Answer: It blocks the traffic, not only alerts. Question three. Which Wi-Fi standard is broken? Answer: W E P.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What is bluesnarfing? Answer: Stealing data from a Bluetooth device without permission. Question five. What is the best defense for I O T devices? Answer: Segment them and change default credentials. Question six. Which firewall decides by application and user? Answer: A next-generation firewall.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Firewalls: packet filter (stateless), stateful, proxy, N G F W, waff, host-based. Rules: default deny; first match wins; egress filtering. I D S or I P S: detect and alert or detect and block. Wi-Fi: W E P broken; W P A two good; W P A three best; enterprise uses eight oh two dot one X. Wi-Fi attacks: rogue A P (unauthorized), evil twin (fake copy). Bluetooth: bluejacking (messages), bluesnarfing (data theft). I O T and I C S: segment, change defaults, patch carefully, inventory.
